solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Turbulent ocean trip up around far side of major capital

indicators.note: turbulent water is churned up, so the letters are stirred
the phrase's letters sit around the extra letter before the mixing
the far side of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
the last letter of majoR

explanation.surface: A rough sea crossing trips up a traveller heading round to a big capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Major' looks like an adjective for the capital, but it only donates its last letter; the capital itself is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the city is the seat of government of Haiti, on the island of Hispaniola.

clue.text: Upper-crust folks look mature

blocks.note: to peer is to look closely
to age is to mature

explanation.surface: Aristocrats are told they look distinguished and mature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look mature' reads as a single phrase about appearance; split it into two verbs, look and mature.
explanation.definitionFit: The peerage is the body of peers, the titled nobility at the top of society.

clue.text: Managed to bring on board staff from part of Africa

indicators.note: bringing something on board puts it inside, so the staff goes inside the verb

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
a wand is a slender staff or rod

explanation.surface: A company managed to recruit staff from an African country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees being hired; here it is a stick, a wand.
explanation.definitionFit: Rwandan means from Rwanda, a country in central-east Africa.

clue.text: Recommendation to split an Italian bubbly and appetisers

indicators.note: the recommendation splits the wine phrase, sitting inside it

blocks.note: AN plus ASTI, the sparkling wine from Piedmont
a tip is a piece of advice or recommendation

explanation.surface: A waiter recommends sharing a bottle of Italian fizz with the starters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An' is taken literally as part of the fodder rather than as an article.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasti are Italian starters served before the main meal.

clue.text: Type of cloth placed beneath piano

indicators.note: in a down entry, the second piece sits below the first

blocks.note: p = piano, soft in music
laid = placed, set down

explanation.surface: A cloth has been laid under a piano to protect the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'beneath' puts LAID below P, so it reads second.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaid is a woollen cloth woven in a tartan or checked pattern.

clue.text: Set up popular booth at farmers’ market?

blocks.note: in = fashionable, popular
a market stall is a booth; the question mark flags it as an example

explanation.surface: A trader sets up a well-liked stand at a farmers' market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up popular booth' reads as one action; 'Set up' is the definition and the rest builds the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: fitting equipment or software in place ready for use is setting it up.

clue.text: Cap requires waterproofing by the sounds of it

indicators.note: tells you to go by how the word is pronounced

blocks.note: sealing keeps water out

explanation.surface: A cap, it seems, needs treating to keep the rain off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cap' reads as a hat that needs waterproofing; it is an upper limit, as in a price cap.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceiling is an upper limit, the same as a cap on spending or prices.

clue.text: Doing business externally, the auditor’s forced to what extent?

indicators.note: an auditor is literally a listener, so this is what the hearer receives

blocks.note: strained = forced; how = to what extent

explanation.surface: An accountant querying a firm's overseas operations wonders how far its figures have been stretched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing business' and 'auditor' paint a company; the business is a pet relieving itself, outdoors rather than in the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A house-trained pet does its business outside, not indoors.

clue.text: Open boxes at the front all contain ham

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it
take only the front letter of each of the following words

blocks.note: overt = open, not concealed
the first letters of All Contain

explanation.surface: An open box of meat has ham packed in every tin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' looks like the meat in the boxes; it is the verb for acting too broadly.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham is to overact, playing a part with exaggeration.

clue.text: Certain Antipodeans in Paris also sense regularly being overlooked

indicators.note: tells you to put the word into French
alternate letters are skipped, keeping the even ones

blocks.note: aussi is French for also
the second and fourth letters of sEnSe

explanation.surface: Some Australians in Paris feel they are being ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooked' tells you which letters go: drop S, N and the final E of sense, keeping E and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Aussies are Australians, and Australia is in the Antipodes.

clue.text: Musician’s skill in this grade sadly lacking, ultimately

indicators.note: things gone sadly have gone wrong, so the letters are rearranged
take the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
the last letter of lackinG

explanation.surface: A music examiner notes that a candidate's skill at this grade is sadly lacking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly lacking' reads as a verdict on the student; 'sadly' is the anagram signal and 'lacking' only gives its G.
explanation.definitionFit: Sight-reading is playing music from a score seen for the first time.

clue.text: Rise of work involving routines?

definitions.note: Rise is a verb, answered by the phrasal verb stand up; the second sense is the noun stand-up.

blocks.note: rise = get to your feet
the routines are a comedian's rehearsed sets of jokes

explanation.surface: A career takes off in a job built around daily routines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Routines' suggests a dull daily grind; it means comedy routines, the sets a stand-up comic performs.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand up is to rise, and stand-up is comedy performed as solo routines.

clue.text: Illegal activity in key London district

blocks.note: D is a musical key
Ealing is a district of west London

explanation.surface: Crime is rife in an important part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' reads as an adjective, important; it is a musical key, D.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the word, used alone, usually means trading in drugs, the classic illegal trade.

clue.text: Marketing gimmick that is canned?

indicators.note: canned things are put inside a tin

blocks.note: i.e. = id est, that is
a can is a tin

explanation.surface: A sales stunt that has been dropped, or perhaps sold in cans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canned' reads as scrapped; it also names the tin that encloses I.E.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-in is a product linked to a film or brand to promote it.

clue.text: Additional information is about ecstasy

indicators.note: turns 'is' round to face the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
ecstasy = great delight

explanation.surface: A note says there is more to learn about the drug ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ecstasy' suggests the drug and its usual letter E; here it means joy, DELIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidelight is incidental information that sheds light on a subject.

clue.text: Casual relationship beginning to destroy marriage

indicators.note: take the first letter of the next word

blocks.note: the first letter of Destroy
an alliance is a union, such as marriage

explanation.surface: A fling starts to wreck a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to destroy' reads as the fling doing damage; it only gives D.
explanation.definitionFit: A dalliance is a casual, not serious, romantic affair.

clue.text: Delicious fresh salami cut by family member

indicators.note: a fresh arrangement makes the letters new
the family member cuts into the salami, going inside it

blocks.note: rearranged
bro is short for brother

explanation.surface: A relative slices into some tasty fresh salami.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' suggests slicing the sausage; it means the brother is inserted into the reshuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosial means tasting or smelling divine, like ambrosia, food of the gods.

clue.text: Somebody very close to you catching a spider?

indicators.note: the friend catches, and so holds, the A

blocks.note: a bestie is a best friend
taken as written

explanation.surface: A best friend catches a spider for you.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark says a spider is only one example of a beastie.
explanation.definitionFit: A beastie is an informal word for a small creature such as an insect or spider.

clue.text: Old ass sent up Herb

indicators.note: in a down entry, sent up means written bottom to top

blocks.note: o = old, as in OT
an onager is a wild ass of Asia

explanation.surface: An old donkey mocks someone called Herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' looks like a man's name being sent up, mocked; it is the plant, and 'sent up' reverses the ass.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: wild marjoram, whose dried leaves flavour pizza and Greek dishes, is one herb among many.

clue.text: Clubs suffer defeat in the ballpark?

blocks.note: C = clubs, the card suit
to lose is to suffer defeat

explanation.surface: Baseball clubs are beaten at the ballpark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the ballpark' reads as the baseball ground; it is the idiom for approximately right, close.
explanation.definitionFit: A guess that is in the ballpark is close to the right figure.

clue.text: Poor excuses from police officers getting dismissed

indicators.note: the police officers get, and so hold, the word for dismissed

blocks.note: cops are police officers
a batsman who is dismissed is out

explanation.surface: Officers who have been sacked offer feeble excuses.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who is dismissed is out.
explanation.definitionFit: A cop-out is a feeble excuse for dodging a responsibility.

clue.text: Character just after small parts

indicators.note: the word for small parts, splits, the other word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: on = immediately after, as in 'on arrival'
micro = very small

explanation.surface: A character comes in just after the bit parts in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' reads as a noun, theatre roles; it is a verb, MICRO parting ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Omicron is a character, the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Greenville’s most impressive breakfast possibly is in N Eastern St

indicators.note: puts the meal word inside the address letters

blocks.note: N as written, E = eastern, St = street
to breakfast is to eat, one example of eating

explanation.surface: A diner on a north-eastern street in Greenville serves the best breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: Greenville is a US city; it flags the American slang sense of neat, meaning excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang neat means great, so the neatest is the most impressive.

clue.text: Firm word of denial upset senior journalist

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset turns the word upside down

blocks.note: not is the word that denies
ed = editor

explanation.surface: A company's denial annoys a top journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as a company; it is the adjective, as in firm muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: exercise leaves muscles and skin taut and firm, which is what toned describes.

clue.text: Current legislator wasn’t honest, as suggested

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
MP = Member of Parliament
lied = was not honest

explanation.surface: A sitting politician was dishonest, as people hinted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' reads as 'present-day'; it is electric current, I in physics.
explanation.definitionFit: To imply something is to suggest it without saying it.

clue.text: Intern bored by editor finally to leave Express?

indicators.note: the intern word is drilled into by the letter, so the letter goes inside
take the last letter of the word before it

blocks.note: to intern is to confine, detain
the last letter of editoR

explanation.surface: A bored newspaper intern wants to quit the Express.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intern' reads as a trainee at the Daily Express newspaper; it is a verb, to confine, and the Express is a fast train.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: an express is one kind of train you might get off.

clue.text: Something free of charge in new German sci-fi franchise

blocks.note: neu is German for new
Tron is a Disney science-fiction film series

explanation.surface: A new German sci-fi series is being given away for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free of charge' reads as costing nothing; it means carrying no electric charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: the subatomic particle in the nucleus carries no electric charge, so is free of it.

clue.text: Support for each number expressing “good for you”

definitions.note: 'you' is a word; second person is the grammatical category it belongs to.

indicators.note: to express is to press out, so G is squeezed out of the number

blocks.note: to second a motion is to support it
per = for each, as in a pound per person
a number is a song; press out G for good

explanation.surface: Someone backs every song that praises the listener with a hearty 'good for you'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expressing' looks like 'saying', introducing the quote; it means squeezing out, so G leaves SONG. 'Number' is a song, not a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: 'You' is the second-person pronoun in grammar.
